questions.a: The President of India
o: A member of the Lok Sabha

questions.q: True or False: Since the Vice President of India is elected, every adult citizen casts a ballot directly for the Vice President. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. The Vice President is chosen through an indirect election: citizens vote for representatives, and those representatives elect the Vice President.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the Vice President is elected indirectly, by representatives whom the citizens elected

questions.q: Compare how a member of the Lok Sabha and the Vice President of India reach office on three points: (a) who votes, (b) whether the election is direct or indirect, (c) which electoral system is used.
questions.a: (a) The citizens of a constituency vote for a Lok Sabha member; the Vice President is voted for by elected representatives, not by citizens directly. (b) The Lok Sabha member is directly elected; the Vice President is indirectly elected. (c) Lok Sabha elections use the First-Past-The-Post system; the Vice President's election uses proportional representation.
s: (a) Citizens vote for the Lok Sabha member; elected representatives vote for the Vice President
(b) Lok Sabha member: direct; Vice President: indirect
(c) Lok Sabha: FPTP; Vice President: proportional representation

questions.q: The Shanti Nagar Residents' Welfare Association holds its committee election on time. But the voters' list used is the old one, so 120 of the colony's 400 households, all of whom moved in recently, are left off it. Only one panel files nominations, and it is declared elected unopposed. The new committee says, 'We were duly elected, so all our decisions are legitimate.' Using the ideas of Fig. 7.1 (equality, accountability, representation, legitimacy) and the chapter's discussion of choice: (a) what percentage of the households had no say in the election? (b) which idea of Fig. 7.1 is hurt by leaving these households off the list, and how? (c) why does a contest with only one panel fail to give the residents a real choice? (d) suggest one rule that would remove both problems at the next election, and (e) judge whether the committee's claim is justified, giving a reason.
questions.a: (a) 120 / 400 x 100 = 30 per cent of the households had no say. (b) Equality and representation: the left-out households are not treated as equals with the others and are not represented on the committee, though its decisions bind them too. (c) The chapter says we cannot exercise our choice if only one party is contesting; with one panel there is nothing to choose between, so residents cannot reject members they do not trust, which also weakens accountability. (d) For example: revise the voters' list before every election so every household is on it, and hold a fresh call for nominations so that more than one panel can contest. (e) Not fully justified: the election was held on time, but with 30 per cent of households excluded and no real choice, the committee's legitimacy is weak; a fair election with a revised list would give it a real mandate.
s: (a) 120 / 400 = 30 per cent with no say
(b) Equality and representation hurt: excluded households have no equal say or representative
(c) One panel means no real choice, so residents cannot reject or hold members accountable
(d) A rule that fixes both: revised voters' list and a genuine contest
(e) Justified judgement on the claim of legitimacy

questions.q: Which electoral system did the framers of the Constitution choose for electing members of the Lok Sabha?
questions.a: The First-Past-The-Post (plurality) system

Elections to the Vidhan Parishad are held by proportional representation through the single transferable vote. III. questions.a: I, II and III

questions.a: (a) The Vidhan Parishad (Legislative Council), the Upper House, and the Vidhan Sabha (Legislative Assembly), the Lower House. (b) Any two of Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana and Uttar Pradesh.
s: (a) Vidhan Parishad (Upper House) and Vidhan Sabha (Lower House)
(b) Any two of Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh

questions.q: Kesarpur is an imaginary country. In its Rampura constituency, 1,00,000 valid votes were polled for three candidates: Lata of the Lotus Party got 41,000 votes, Vikram of the Wheel Party got 36,000 and Salma of the Kite Party got 23,000. Kesarpur's Election Board wants to know how this result would look under the three electoral systems described in the chapter. (a) Under First-Past-The-Post, who wins Rampura? (b) What percentage of the votes did the winner get, and is it more than half? (c) Under the majority system, does anyone win in the first round? If not, who goes to the second round? (d) Suppose these were the three parties' shares of the national vote in a 100-seat house elected by proportional representation. How many seats would each party get?
questions.a: (a) Lata wins, because she has the most votes. (b) 41,000 of 1,00,000 is 41 per cent, which is less than half; under FPTP she still wins. (c) No one crosses 50 per cent, so no one wins in round 1; the top two, Lata and Vikram, compete in the second round. (d) Seats are given in proportion to votes: Lotus 41, Wheel 36, Kite 23.
s: (a) Lata wins under FPTP (most votes)
(b) 41 per cent, less than half, yet enough under FPTP
(c) No one above 50 per cent; Lata and Vikram go to round 2
(d) Lotus 41, Wheel 36, Kite 23 seats

questions.q: Assertion (A): Under First-Past-The-Post, a candidate can win a seat with less than half of the votes polled. Reason (R): Under the majority system, a candidate who does not get more than 50 per cent of the votes must face a second round. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.a: 24 seats

questions.q: In a constituency, four candidates P, Q, R and S get 31, 27, 24 and 18 per cent of the votes. (a) Who wins under First-Past-The-Post, and why? (b) What would happen instead under the majority system?
questions.a: (a) P wins, because under FPTP the candidate with the most votes wins even with less than 50 per cent. (b) No one has more than 50 per cent, so the top two, P and Q, would compete again in a second round.
s: (a) P wins: most votes is enough under FPTP
(b) No one above 50 per cent, so P and Q go to a second round

questions.q: Arjun says, 'The Vidhan Parishad is elected just like the Vidhan Sabha: all adult voters of the State choose its members by First-Past-The-Post.' Is he right? Explain using the chapter.
questions.a: No. The Vidhan Sabha is directly elected by FPTP, but the Vidhan Parishad is not. Its members are elected by the members of the Vidhan Sabha and of local bodies, and by graduates and teachers of the State, while the Governor nominates some members for fields such as art, science, literature, social service and co-operatives. Its elections use proportional representation by single transferable vote, not FPTP.
s: Verdict: Arjun is wrong; only the Vidhan Sabha is directly elected by FPTP
Vidhan Parishad electors: Vidhan Sabha members, local bodies, graduates and teachers, plus members nominated by the Governor
Its system is proportional representation by single transferable vote

questions.q: A Vidhan Parishad election by single transferable vote must fill 2 seats. There are 60,000 valid votes. First-preference votes: A 21,500, B 17,000, C 12,300 and D 9,200. On D's ballots, the second preferences are B 3,400 and C 5,800. Using the chapter's quota rule, quota = (total valid votes divided by (seats + 1)) + 1, and its counting steps: (a) find the quota, (b) say who is elected on the first count, (c) say who is eliminated and what happens to those votes, (d) find the new totals and say who fills the second seat.
questions.a: (a) Quota = 60,000 / 3 + 1 = 20,001. (b) A has 21,500, which is more than 20,001, so A is elected on the first count. (c) D has the lowest votes and is eliminated; D's 9,200 votes go to the second preferences: 3,400 to B and 5,800 to C. (d) B now has 17,000 + 3,400 = 20,400 and C has 12,300 + 5,800 = 18,100. B reaches the quota and fills the second seat; C is not elected.
s: (b) A elected first, as 21,500 is above the quota
(c) D eliminated; 3,400 votes go to B and 5,800 to C
(d) B 20,400 (reaches quota, elected), C 18,100 (not elected)

questions.q: Which law lays down the rules for the nomination of candidates, election campaigns and voting procedures?
questions.a: The Representation of the People Act, 1951
o: The Representation of the People Act, 1951
The Representation of the People Act, 1950
The Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952

questions.q: Which Article of the Constitution of India mandates the setting up of a Delimitation Commission?
questions.a: Article 82

questions.q: True or False: Delimitation fixes both the number of seats in each state and the boundaries of constituencies for elections to the Lok Sabha and the Vidhan Sabha. Give a reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter defines delimitation as the process of determining the number of seats and fixing the territorial boundaries in each state for Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha elections.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: delimitation determines the number of seats and fixes constituency boundaries for both houses

questions.q: Answer in one line each. (a) What is delimitation? (b) What ratio does delimitation try to keep as close to equal as possible across constituencies? (c) Why do constituency boundaries need to change over time?
questions.a: (a) The process of determining the number of seats and fixing the territorial boundaries of constituencies in each state for Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha elections. (b) The ratio of seats to population. (c) Because population density shifts over time, so boundaries fixed earlier no longer give equal representation.
s: (a) Determining the number of seats and fixing constituency boundaries
(b) The ratio of seats to population
(c) Shifts in population density over time

questions.q: For each campaign incident below, say whether it is a corrupt practice listed in the Representation of the People Act, 1951, and name the rule it breaks (or say why it is allowed). (a) A candidate hands out pressure cookers to voters in a basti. (b) A candidate tells a gathering to vote for her because she speaks the same language as them. (c) A candidate's agent asks an excise officer of the district to hand out the candidate's pamphlets. (d) A candidate holds a public meeting to explain her plan for a new water pipeline. (e) A candidate's agent, with her consent, promises a young voter Rs 2,000 to stay at home on polling day.
questions.a: (a) Corrupt practice: a gift to voters to make them vote. (b) Corrupt practice: appealing for votes on the basis of language. (c) Corrupt practice: taking assistance in favour of the candidate from government-related personnel, which includes excise officers. (d) Not a corrupt practice: explaining a programme is ordinary campaigning. (e) Corrupt practice: a promise made with the candidate's consent to make a person refrain from voting.
s: (a) Corrupt: gift to influence voting
(b) Corrupt: appeal on the basis of language
(c) Corrupt: assistance from an excise officer (government-related personnel)
(d) Allowed: campaigning on a programme
(e) Corrupt: promise to make a person refrain from voting

questions.q: Read the statements. I. The Representation of the People Act, 1950 lays down the rules for election campaigns. II. The Representation of the People Act, 1951 deals with post-election disputes. III. Delimitation applies to constituencies of both the Lok Sabha and the Vidhan Sabha. Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only

questions.q: Match each problem with the law or body that deals with it. 1. A body set up as Article 82 of the Constitution requires must redraw constituency boundaries after population shifts 2. A citizen who has turned 18 finds her name missing from the electoral roll 3. A losing candidate disputes the result after counting 4. The election of the Vice President a. The Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952 b. The Delimitation Commission c. The Representation of the People Act, 1951 d. The Representation of the People Act, 1950

Rahul says, 'The Representation of the People Act, 1950 alone governs an Indian election, from making the voters' list to settling disputes after the result.' Is he right? Explain with what each Act covers.
questions.a: No. The 1950 Act deals mainly with allocation of seats and delimitation, the preparation and revision of electoral rolls, and the right of every citizen of 18 and above to vote without discrimination. The 1951 Act covers all other aspects: nomination of candidates, campaigns, voting procedures, electoral offences and corrupt practices, and post-election disputes. The two Acts together ensure integrity, transparency and accountability.
s: Verdict: No, two Acts share the work
1950 Act: seats, delimitation, electoral rolls, right to vote at 18
1951 Act: nominations, campaigns, voting, offences and corrupt practices, disputes

questions.q: A candidate's cousin, without her knowledge or consent, distributes blankets to voters. Her rival says, 'She has committed a corrupt practice under the RPA, 1951.' Using the chapter's wording of this corrupt practice, analyse whether the rival's claim is established by these facts alone, and say what fact would change the answer.
questions.a: The chapter describes this corrupt practice as a gift, offer or promise made by a candidate, or with the candidate's consent, to make a person vote or refrain from voting. Distributing blankets to voters is a gift of that kind. But here it was done without her knowledge or consent, so by the chapter's wording the claim against her is not established by these facts alone. If it were shown that she consented to the gifts, the act would be a corrupt practice on her behalf.
s: States the rule: gift by the candidate or with her consent, to influence voting
Applies it: the gift fits, but without her consent the claim is not established
Names the deciding fact: proof of her consent would make it a corrupt practice

questions.q: An imaginary state has four Lok Sabha constituencies with 14, 18, 26 and 32 lakh people. A new delimitation gives the state five seats, and the Delimitation Commission must redraw the boundaries so that the ratio of seats to population is as close to equal as possible. (a) What is the ideal population per constituency with five seats? (b) Which existing constituency already matches this ideal? (c) The 32-lakh constituency is split into two, one part with 18 lakh people. How many people are in the other part, and how far is it from the ideal? (d) After the split, which constituency is furthest from the ideal, and how could the Commission move areas between neighbouring constituencies so that all five match it?
questions.a: (a) Total = 14 + 18 + 26 + 32 = 90 lakh; 90 / 5 = 18 lakh. (b) The 18-lakh constituency. (c) 32 - 18 = 14 lakh, which is 4 lakh below the ideal. (d) The 26-lakh constituency, 8 lakh above the ideal. If it hands 4 lakh people to each of the two 14-lakh constituencies next to it, it falls to 26 - 8 = 18 lakh and each of them rises to 14 + 4 = 18 lakh, so all five constituencies have 18 lakh.
s: (a) 90 lakh / 5 = 18 lakh
(b) The 18-lakh constituency matches
(c) 32 - 18 = 14 lakh, 4 lakh below the ideal
(d) 26-lakh seat is 8 lakh above; move 4 lakh to each 14-lakh seat so all are 18 lakh

questions.q: Name the ECI facility that fits each person, and say in a few words why. (a) Havildar Joseph, a service voter, is posted in Ladakh, but his name is on the roll of a constituency in Kerala. (b) Kamla Devi is 87 years old and cannot walk to the polling station. (c) Imran, a registered voter with a benchmark disability of 50 per cent, cannot travel to his polling station on polling day. A friend tells him to use the Saksham App. Which facility actually lets him cast his vote, and why is the Saksham App not enough?
questions.a: (a) ETPBS: as a service voter he can receive and cast a postal ballot electronically from outside his constituency. (b) Voting from home, which is available to senior citizens above 85 years of age. (c) Voting from home, which is also available to persons with disabilities with a benchmark disability of 40 per cent; the Saksham App only helps PwDs register and find their polling station, so it does not let him vote without going there.
s: (a) ETPBS for a service voter outside his constituency
(b) Voting from home for a voter above 85
(c) Voting from home (benchmark disability of 40 per cent or more); Saksham only helps with registration and finding the station

questions.q: The five-year term of the Vidhan Sabha of an imaginary state, Suryaprant, ends on 30 May. The ECI is choosing one week for polling. Window 1 (2-8 March): Class 10 and 12 board examinations are on, and many school buildings are used as polling stations. Window 2 (12-18 April): the wheat harvest is at its peak, and 55 per cent of voters belong to farming families. Window 3 (6-12 May): examinations and the harvest are over, but afternoon temperatures reach 44 degrees Celsius, and a major festival falls on 9 May. (a) Why must the ECI hold this election before 30 May? (b) Which factor from the chapter's list rules out Window 1, and which rules out Window 2? (c) Name the two factors that make Window 3 difficult. (d) Choose a window and justify your choice using the data.
questions.a: (a) The constitutionally mandated term of the legislature is five years; when it ends, the ECI must conduct an election. (b) Window 1 clashes with school examination schedules (and school buildings are needed); Window 2 clashes with the agricultural cycle, when 55 per cent of voters are busy with the harvest. (c) Weather conditions (44 degrees Celsius heat) and a festival on 9 May. (d) A justified choice, for example: Window 3 on days other than 9 May, because exams and the harvest affect large numbers throughout their windows, while the festival can be avoided by choosing other dates in the week and heat is a smaller barrier than missing the harvest or the exams. A choice of another window earns the mark only if it weighs the data honestly.
s: (a) The five-year term ends, so the ECI must hold the election
(b) Window 1: examination schedules; Window 2: agricultural cycle
(c) Window 3: weather conditions and a festival
(d) A choice justified by weighing the data of all three windows

questions.q: With over 96.8 crore eligible voters, the ECI relies on a digital ecosystem (Fig. 7.6) that serves voters, candidates and election officials. (a) Name two apps that serve voters and say what each does. (b) Name one app that serves candidates and political parties and what it offers. (c) Name one system that serves election officials and what it does. (d) Judge which of the three groups gains the most from this ecosystem in conducting free and fair elections, and give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Any two: Voter Helpline App (registration, transposition, verification, election information); cVIGIL App (report Model Code of Conduct violations within minutes, so flying squads reach the spot using auto location); Saksham App (helps persons with disabilities register and find polling stations); ETPBS (lets service voters cast postal ballots electronically). (b) Suvidha: nomination forms and updates, and permissions for meetings, rallies, vehicles and loudspeakers with real-time status. (c) ERONET (processing forms and maintaining E-Rolls) or Sugam (managing vehicles requisitioned for election work). (d) A justified judgement, for example voters, because tools like cVIGIL and Saksham let ordinary people report misconduct and take part regardless of disability, which is what makes elections free and inclusive; or officials, because efficient rolls and logistics make an exercise of this size possible.
s: (a) First voter app named with its use
(a) Second voter app named with its use
(b) Suvidha and what it offers candidates
(c) ERONET or Sugam and what it does for officials
(d) Justified judgement of which group gains most

questions.a: I and II only

questions.q: Assertion (A): The chapter treats every act of defection as political opportunism. Reason (R): The purpose of the Anti-Defection Law is to prevent defection and so provide stability to the elected government. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q: True or False: The Anti-Defection Law applies only to Members of Parliament; members of a State Assembly are outside it. Give a reason.
questions.a: False. The law covers a member of the Parliament or of a State Assembly: either can be disqualified from the respective House for defection.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: the law names members of the Parliament or a State Assembly, so both are covered

questions.q: Meena, an MLA elected on Party P's ticket, votes against Party P's whip on a Bill but stays a member of Party P. Ravi, another MLA elected on Party P's ticket, resigns from Party P and joins Party Q. Their friend Asha says, 'Only Ravi has defected, because Meena has not left the party.' (a) Is Asha right about Meena? Use the chapter's meaning of defection. (b) What can the Speaker of the House do about Meena and Ravi under the Anti-Defection Law? (c) Name one way in which defection can still be viewed positively, according to the chapter.
questions.a: (a) No: the chapter says defection includes choosing to act independently of the party's decisions, particularly in voting in the legislature, so Meena's vote against the whip is also defection, even though she did not switch parties. (b) Under the Anti-Defection Law, a member who votes against the party's whip or voluntarily gives up party membership can be disqualified from the House; the Speaker decides in such cases, so Meena and Ravi can both be disqualified. (c) It can be viewed as a way to uphold conscience or respond to changing public expectations.
s: (a) Not right: acting independently in voting is also defection, not only joining another party
(b) Both can be disqualified for voting against the whip or leaving the party; the Speaker decides
(c) Defection can uphold conscience or respond to changing public expectations

questions.q: In a 250-seat Vidhan Sabha, Party K wins 140 seats, Party L wins 85 and others win 25. A party needs more than half the seats, that is 126, to form a government on its own. Using Fig. 7.11 and the Anti-Defection Law: (a) which party forms the government and which is the opposition? (b) according to Fig. 7.11, what two things does the winning party do? (c) name two ways the opposition ensures accountability. (d) Later, 20 members of Party K voluntarily give up their party membership. What can happen to them, and who decides? While the House still has 250 members, before the decision is made, how many seats does Party K now hold, and is that more than 126?
questions.a: (a) Party K (140, above 126) forms the government; Party L is the opposition. (b) It forms the government, and it formulates and implements policies. (c) The opposition ensures accountability by participating in debates and in committees. (d) The 20 members can be disqualified from the House; the Speaker decides. Before the decision, with the House still at 250 members, Party K holds 140 - 20 = 120 seats, which is fewer than 126, so it no longer has a majority on its own.
s: (a) K forms the government (140 > 126), L is the opposition
(b) Forms the government and formulates and implements policies
(c) Opposition: debates and committees to ensure accountability
(d) Can be disqualified, Speaker decides; 120 seats, fewer than 126

questions.q: Fig. 7.13 shows the road to free and fair elections with potholes marking the challenges. Which of these is shown as a challenge on that road?
questions.a: Intimidation

questions.q: About how many voters did India conduct elections for in 2024, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Over 96.8 crore

questions.q: The chapter says that casting a vote is 'a constitutional right as well as a duty of every citizen'. (a) What does it mean that voting is a right? (b) What does it mean that voting is a duty?
questions.a: (a) As a right, the Constitution gives every citizen the right to vote, the principal means by which we choose our representatives. (b) As a duty, a citizen is expected to actually cast the vote, fulfilling her responsibility as a citizen, since elections give every citizen an equal voice in forming a government.
s: (a) Right: the Constitution gives every citizen the right to vote and choose representatives
(b) Duty: a citizen is expected to cast the vote as her responsibility, so that every citizen has a voice

questions.q: Name the measure from the chapter that fits each need. (a) A visually impaired voter wants to cast her vote on the machine without help. (b) The rules whose violations a voter can report on the cVIGIL App. (c) The Act that lists corrupt practices, such as a gift to a voter to make her vote.
questions.a: (a) The EVM with Braille. (b) The Model Code of Conduct. (c) The Representation of the People Act, 1951.
s: (a) EVM with Braille
(b) Model Code of Conduct
(c) Representation of the People Act, 1951

questions.q: Four things happen in Chandanpur in the week before polling. For each, name the challenge or the measure from the chapter that fits. (a) A post shared widely on social media falsely claims that voters can now cast their vote by sending a text message. (b) Some men stand near a hamlet and warn residents that they will be harmed if they vote. (c) Late at night a party's loudspeaker van is still playing campaign songs, though its permission for loudspeakers ended at 10 pm; a resident wants a flying squad sent to the spot. Which ECI app should she use? (d) Volunteers go door to door telling people how and where to vote; which measure is this?
questions.a: (a) Misinformation or fake news. (b) Intimidation. (c) The cVIGIL App, with which voters report Model Code of Conduct violations and election misconduct, and flying squads reach the spot using auto location. (d) A voters' awareness campaign.
s: (a) Misinformation or fake news
(b) Intimidation
(c) cVIGIL App
(d) Voters' awareness campaign

questions.q: Assertion (A): Conducting elections in India is a challenging task. Reason (R): The ECI addresses challenges such as misinformation and intimidation through the Model Code of Conduct, among other measures. Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: In the village of Kherwa, a local gang has warned families that they will be harmed if they go to vote. A student says, 'The VVPAT will solve Kherwa's problem.' Why is this response weak?
questions.a: The VVPAT lets a voter check the vote she has cast, but it cannot help voters who are kept away from the booth by fear.
o: The VVPAT lets a voter check the vote she has cast, but it cannot help voters who are kept away from the booth by fear.
The VVPAT is used only in by-elections, not in general elections.
Intimidation is not one of the challenges the chapter names.
The VVPAT is meant only for persons with disabilities.

questions.q: In one ward, Booth A has 1,250 voters on its roll and 900 of them voted; Booth B has 1,600 voters and 880 of them voted. (a) Find the turnout of each booth as a percentage. (b) A voters' awareness campaign can cover only one booth first. Which booth should it cover, and by how many percentage points is that booth behind the other?
questions.a: (a) Booth A: 900 / 1,250 x 100 = 72 per cent; Booth B: 880 / 1,600 x 100 = 55 per cent. (b) Booth B, which is 72 - 55 = 17 percentage points behind; it also has more people who did not vote (720 against 350).
s: (a) Booth A 72 per cent, Booth B 55 per cent
(b) Booth B, 17 percentage points behind

questions.q: Sonpur constituency has 1,50,000 voters. At a planning meeting a week before polling, the District Election Officer of Sonpur reviews three findings. (i) A video spreading on phones falsely claims that the EVMs in Sonpur have been pre-set for one party. (ii) In a hamlet of 400 voters, a group has warned people not to come out on polling day. (iii) A survey finds that 30 per cent of first-time voters do not know how they can check their vote. The district can pay for only one extra step: a police patrol for the hamlet, or a constituency-wide awareness drive. (a) Name the challenge in finding (i) and in finding (ii). (b) Which measure from the chapter answers the doubt in findings (i) and (iii)? (c) What percentage of Sonpur's voters live in the hamlet? (d) Which step should the district choose? Justify using your answers.
questions.a: (a) (i) Misinformation or fake news; (ii) intimidation. (b) VVPAT, which lets each voter see a slip of the vote cast, supported by a voters' awareness campaign explaining it. (c) 400 / 1,50,000 x 100 = about 0.27 per cent. (d) A justified decision, for example: the patrol, because the hamlet is small but intimidation takes away the right to vote itself, and no awareness drive can protect those 400 voters; or the awareness drive, because the false video and the 30 per cent of unsure first-time voters reach the whole constituency, while the hamlet is only about 0.27 per cent of voters.
s: (a) (i) misinformation or fake news; (ii) intimidation
(b) VVPAT with voter awareness
(c) About 0.27 per cent
(d) Decision justified using the scale (0.27 per cent) against the seriousness of intimidation

questions.q: The chapter asks, 'Why should you vote?' and gives four reasons: (A) the opportunity to choose my representative; (B) it makes me a responsible person; (C) the opportunity to change a non-performing representative; (D) it strengthens democracy. Arrange the four in descending order of your choice. Then, for each reason, link it to one idea from the chapter (such as accountability, a right and a duty, periodic elections, informed choice, or elections as the soul of democracy), and justify why your first choice comes first.
questions.a: Any order with sound links, for example D, C, A, B. D: elections are the soul of democracy because they give every citizen an equal voice in forming a government. C: periodic elections keep representatives accountable, since the vote can replace one who does not perform. A: the vote is the principal means of exercising the right to elect, and parties help voters make an informed choice. B: casting a vote is a duty as well as a constitutional right. Justification of the first choice, for example: D comes first because the other three, choosing, replacing and acting responsibly, all add up to a stronger democracy.
s: Reason A linked to a chapter idea (right to elect, informed choice)
Reason B linked to a chapter idea (vote as a duty)
Reason C linked to a chapter idea (accountability through periodic elections)
Reason D linked to a chapter idea (soul of democracy, equal voice)
Order given and first choice justified
